evidence.claim: Follow wagon ruts from a Snake River crossing toward Boise.
evidence.quote: The Main Oregon Trail Back Country Byway follows the main Oregon Trail from the crossing of the Snake River near Glenns Ferry to Bonneville Point, southeast of Boise.

evidence.claim: The Main Oregon Trail Back Country Byway links paved and gravel roads across the sagebrush desert between Glenns Ferry and Bonneville Point, southeast of Boise.
evidence.quote: All of the Byway roads are paved or good gravel roads.

evidence.claim: across the sagebrush desert between Glenns Ferry and Bonneville Point, southeast of Boise.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management presents this 102-mile backcountry route as a way to see Oregon Trail ruts and reach sections on foot.
evidence.quote: The total distance of the byway is 102 miles.

evidence.claim: as a way to see Oregon Trail ruts and reach sections on foot.
evidence.quote: Oregon Trail ruts are visible along much of this route. Several locations allow access for hiking and horseback riding on the Oregon Trail.

evidence.claim: Its suggested eight-hour trip from Boise includes the state park’s interpretive center and stops along the trail.
evidence.quote: Allow eight hours to complete the trip from Boise, including time to visit the Three Island Crossing State Park interpretive center and to view the Oregon Trail at the various access points along the way.

evidence.claim: The trail from Three Island Crossing to Boise carried the main emigrant traffic during the Oregon Trail’s first ten years.
evidence.quote: The main Oregon Trail from Three Island Crossing to Boise was the primary route utilized by the emigrants for the first 10 years of the trail.

evidence.claim: Travelers unable to cross the Snake River followed the South Alternate instead.
evidence.quote: Those emigrants who could not cross the Snake River were forced to follow the south side of the Snake River using a route called the South Alternate.

evidence.claim: Freight wagons and stagecoaches later used much of the trail to connect with the railroad in northern Utah, and trail travel continued into the early 1900s.
evidence.quote: Freight and stage roads to the railroad in northern Utah utilized much of the Oregon Trail for many years. The Oregon Trail continued to be used long after the building of the railroads across southern Idaho, even into the early 1900s.

evidence.claim: Begin with the loop from Glenns Ferry to the south-bank bluffs above Three Island Crossing, then return to the state park on the north bank.
evidence.quote: Part 1 of the byway is a loop drive that takes you to the south side of the Snake River to view the Three Island Crossing location from the bluffs above the river, and then ends on the north side of the river at Three Island Crossing State Park interpretive center.

evidence.claim: County roads continue toward Rattlesnake Creek and Canyon Creek Stage Station before reaching Bonneville Point.
evidence.quote: The Byway is separated into three parts—The Snake River and Three Island Crossing State Park, The Snake River to Rattlesnake Creek, and Rattlesnake Creek to Bonneville Point.

evidence.claim: and Canyon Creek Stage Station
evidence.quote: Mile 23.9—Interpretive sign. The historic Canyon Creek Stage Station

evidence.claim: Near Ditto Creek, large granite boulders and grassier hillsides mark a change in the landscape before the trail descends into the narrow creek valley.
evidence.quote: The landscape changes to include large granite boulders and more grass on the hillsides before the trail drops down and crosses the narrow Ditto Creek valley.

evidence.claim: At Bonneville Point, trail ruts marked with concrete posts lead into the story of the descent toward the Boise River valley.
evidence.quote: Excellent ruts marked by concrete posts are available for hiking in the area.

evidence.claim: the descent toward the Boise River valley.
evidence.quote: The trail descended into the river valley, dropping over several benches along the way.

evidence.claim: Wagon ruts remain between the Snake River and the park’s History and Education Center.
evidence.quote: Oregon Trail ruts are visible between the river and the Center.

evidence.claim: Despite the crossing’s name, emigrants used only two of the three islands to ford the river.
evidence.quote: Although there are three islands at this location, only two were used in the crossing.

evidence.claim: Strong currents, deep water and concealed holes made the crossing dangerous and caused drownings.
evidence.quote: Strong currents, deep water, and hidden holes caused difficulties and drownings as the emigrants forded the Snake River here.

evidence.claim: Those who feared the ford continued along the rough, dry South Alternate.
evidence.quote: Those who feared to cross were forced to continue down the south side of the Snake River over a rough and dry route known as the South Alternate.

evidence.claim: The park opened in 1971 to interpret the crossing; the byway loop also reaches an overlook with interpretive signs on the opposite bluff.
evidence.quote: was formally opened to the public as a state park in 1971.

evidence.claim: the byway loop also reaches an overlook with interpretive signs on the opposite bluff.
evidence.quote: A stop may be made on the bluff overlooking the site of Three Island Crossing where interpretive signs are available.

evidence.claim: The center interprets the Oregon Trail with exhibits and a film, while the ruts place the crossing story on the ground.
evidence.quote: The center shows a film about the Oregon Trail. It has excellent displays and a gift shop.

evidence.claim: BLM asks drivers to avoid trail access roads when wet or muddy; high-clearance vehicles may be required off the byway.
evidence.quote: High-clearance vehicles may be required to access the trail off the byway. Four-wheel drive is not needed to travel the byway, but please avoid the access roads if they are wet or muddy.

evidence.claim: The builders of Canyon Creek’s stone stage station used deer hair to bind its mortar.
evidence.quote: The mortar used deer hair to hold the rocks together.

evidence.claim: Built by the Archibald Daniel family in 1874, it had separate buildings for cooking and sleeping.
evidence.quote: the station was built in 1874 by the Archibald Daniel family.

evidence.claim: it had separate buildings for cooking and sleeping.
evidence.quote: The station consisted of two buildings, the north building was the cooking building, the south was the sleeping building.

evidence.claim: Travelers could obtain meals, water and fresh horses before the station became a home and working farm.
evidence.quote: including hot meals, fruits and vegetables, meats, cool water, fresh horses for the mail and sweet grass for livestock until 1884, when the Oregon Shortline Railroad was completed. After that, it served as a home and working farm.

evidence.claim: A 1976 fire left only the stone walls.
evidence.quote: A fire badly gutted the structure in 1976, leaving only the rock walls standing.

evidence.claim: Restoration rebuilt walls in 2016 and 2017 and added a roof in 2018.
evidence.quote: The gable ends and north wall were completed in 2016, and the south wall was rebuilt in 2017. In 2018, the roof was installed

evidence.claim: Emigrants called this valley Barrel Creek for its round shape and surrounding rock walls.
evidence.quote: The creek was often called “Barrel Creek” due to the round shape of the valley and the steep rock walls which surround the valley.

evidence.claim: The grounds were deeded to the Bureau of Land Management in 2015 for preservation.
evidence.quote: The area of the stage station has been deeded to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) in 2015 for preservation.

evidence.claim: Concrete posts mark Oregon Trail ruts at Bonneville Point, where the wagon route reached a ridge above the Boise River valley.
evidence.quote: Excellent ruts marked by concrete posts are available for hiking in the area.

evidence.claim: For emigrants, this was their first view of that valley.
evidence.quote: As the trail crossed a ridge, the emigrants were treated to their first view of the Boise River valley.

evidence.claim: The river’s cottonwoods were the first substantial trees along the trail for several weeks.
evidence.quote: the river flowed through a large valley lined with cottonwood trees. These were the first significant trees along the trail for several weeks.

evidence.claim: From the ridge, the trail dropped over a succession of benches toward the river.
evidence.quote: The trail descended into the river valley, dropping over several benches along the way.

evidence.claim: Interpretive signs and historical monuments stand at the point, and the marked ruts are available for hiking.
evidence.quote: There are a number of interpretive signs and historical monuments at Bonneville Point. Excellent ruts marked by concrete posts are available for hiking in the area.
